summary.text: 都 is a city character built from 邑, the settlement element, and 者, a sound element. Its bronze-inscription use is reported for a city; the commonly listed city and capital senses belong to the dū reading. The separate dōu reading means “all,” whose proposed connection to 諸 remains unverified.

formation.text: A phonosemantic compound: 邑 contributes the settlement or city category, while 者 supplies a sound cue for the city reading. The analysis is reported for bronze inscriptions and in the traditional lexicographic account. The latter describes a settlement with a former ruler’s ancestral temple, but does not establish that as the earliest spoken meaning or the graph’s ultimate pictorial origin.

components.text: In 都, 邑 is the settlement or city element. The traditional analysis assigns it the meaning contribution; no earlier distinct form or detailed graphic history is established here.

者 is the sound element in 都’s city reading. The historical comparison shows related, though not identical, reconstructed syllables; the sound data support this role without proving the ultimate origin of the graph.

sound.text: Old Chinese comparisons in Zhengzhang’s system: 者 *tjaːʔ and 都 *taː. Their related initials and finals are consistent with a sound cue, although the reconstructed forms are not identical.

history.text: Reported bronze witnesses include a Western Zhou inscription associated with the 㝬鐘 and later Spring and Autumn examples. These reports support an early city use and the component analysis, but the glyph images were not visually inspected and do not establish stroke-by-stroke change or a pictorial origin. No oracle-bone form was established in the research summarized here.

The traditional lexicographic account describes a 都 as an 邑 containing a former ruler’s ancestral temple. The cited classical references also report territorial or fief, large-city, and capital uses. They do not securely date those senses or establish a precise path among them.

The dōu reading “all” is a separate word use of the whole graph, not a meaning shown to develop from the city sense. A proposal relates it to 諸 on the basis of colloquial usage, but the early sound match and borrowing are not independently established in this research. The city reading’s phonetic element 者 is a distinct matter.

uncertainties.text: The original pictorial referent, any earlier graphic form, and detailed changes in the written shape are unresolved by the inspected evidence; modern appearance alone cannot settle them.
The reported senses “elegant,” “great,” “inhabit,” and “gather” are not connected by an established chronology or semantic path in this evidence.
The proposed relationship between dōu “all” and 諸 lacks an independently established early pronunciation comparison and borrowing history here.

senses.period: Western Zhou bronze use reported; exact dating of the spoken sense unresolved
senses.text: A bronze inscription associated with the 㝬鐘 is reported to use 都 for a city. This supports an early city use, but not the claim that “city” was the first spoken meaning.

senses.gloss: settlement containing a former ruler’s ancestral temple
senses.period: Han lexicographic account; underlying spoken sense dating unresolved
senses.text: The traditional dictionary account defines 都 as an 邑 with the former ruler’s ancestral temple. This is an attested lexicographic explanation, not proof of the word’s earliest meaning.
A cited Zhou ritual text reports 都 as a territorial or fief category. The evidence does not establish its chronological relation to the shrine-bearing settlement sense.
Classical citations report large-city and capital uses. Their chronology relative to the institutional settlement and fief senses is not established here.

senses.period: Reported in a lexicographic source; exact earliest attestation unresolved
senses.text: The totalizing word is written 都 and read dōu in Mandarin. Its proposed relationship to 諸 is a word-level borrowing account, not a demonstrated extension of the city meaning.
A classical citation records an elegant or beautiful sense. The evidence does not establish how it relates to the settlement or city senses.
The character is currently read dū for the city and capital meanings.
The character is also currently read dōu for “all” or “the whole”; the word’s proposed historical relation to 諸 remains unverified here.

limitations.text: The cited senses do not by themselves establish transitions among shrine settlement, fief, large city, capital, elegance, and totalizing meaning.
The early history and sound basis of the proposed 諸-to-dōu relationship were not independently verified in the research summarized here.
The earliest reported bronze city use does not prove that “city” was the earliest spoken meaning; the shrine-bearing definition is a later lexicographic account.

overview.text: 都 combines a settlement element with a sound element to write the city word. Its dōu reading “all” is a separate word; a proposed link to 諸 would depend on similar sound, but that historical match remains unverified.

components.text: 邑 marks the settlement or city category in this character.
者 supplies a sound cue for the city reading; its reconstructed form is related to, but not identical with, 都’s.

takeaway.text: The “all” reading is a separate word use; its proposed borrowing from 諸 is not established here.

relationships.text: 邑 contributes the settlement or city category in the reported analysis of 都.
者 supplies the sound cue for the city reading; the reported Old Chinese comparisons support a phonetic relationship despite differences in reconstructed syllable details.
